turns.speaker: tutor
turns.text: What is 1/2 + 1/3?

turns.speaker: tutor
turns.text: How did you get 2/5?

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: I added the top and the bottom numbers. 1 plus 1 is 2 and 2 plus 3 is 5.

turns.speaker: tutor
turns.text: Is 2/5 bigger or smaller than 1/2?

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: smaller i think. that is weird because I added more.

turns.speaker: tutor
turns.text: Good noticing. Let's cut a roti into halves and thirds and see what size the pieces are.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: the half piece and the third piece are not the same size so I cant just count them.

turns.speaker: tutor
turns.text: What is 2/7 + 3/7?

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: 5/7 because the pieces are already the same size, sevenths.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: I need a common denominator. 1/2 is 2/4 so it is 3/4.

turns.speaker: tutor
turns.text: What about 2/3 + 1/4?

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: 3/7? no wait. the denominators are different. 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.

turns.speaker: tutor
turns.text: Last week we added fractions. Can you explain to a friend why 1/2 + 1/3 is not 2/5?

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Because halves and thirds are different sized pieces. You change both to sixths first, 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. 2/5 is less than 1/2 so it cant be the answer.

turns.speaker: tutor
turns.text: Which is bigger, 1/8 or 1/6?

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: 1/6, because sixths are bigger pieces than eighths.

turns.speaker: tutor
turns.text: What is 0.3 x 0.2?

turns.speaker: tutor
turns.text: Is that bigger or smaller than 0.3?

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: bigger. but multiplying by 0.2 is like taking a part of it so it should be smaller. maybe 0.06?
